pos.personaBrief: Uruguay gave Brazil the ball in the first half and defended, then hit fast on the wings (Ghiggia, long balls luring the European press vs Spain), though it also kept cadenced midfield touch and took control after the break. Control came from danger and the midfield, not possession counts.

pro.personaBrief: The Spain game used long launches that paid off at 29 minutes, and Ghiggia's pace on the right was the main weapon, with sharp quick transitions. Build-up was simple and forward in a WM era.

est.personaBrief: A classic WM with set positions and wide wingers holding the flank (Ghiggia down the right), with Varela and the half-backs covering their sectors. Little positional interchange or tight rondo-style play is documented.

lar.personaBrief: Ghiggia down the right scored in all four games, including the winner, and Lance cites the pace of the wingers as the transition weapon. The attack was built on wide pace and crosses and cut-ins, with a diagonal run after a one-two.

blo.personaBrief: López wanted a defensive plan against Brazil and the team held a deep line in the first half, with Máspoli the hero. Forwards did not press high, and the pressing only came after Varela demanded advanced lines.

mar.personaBrief: Lance describes González and Tejera marking Zarra closely, and Wilson (unverified) has the wing-halves man-marking Brazil's wingers. This is the WM era of man-to-man marking.

pla.personaBrief: López planned a defensive approach specifically for the powerful Brazilian attack, adapting to the opponent, and Máspoli's request about crosses was handled on the spot. Varela's rebuttal came from a player, not the coach's identity.

res.personaBrief: A draw would not have been enough for Uruguay, but the club officials asked only for a decorous loss and the team won by grit (garra). The mentality was win, with results valued over show and a defensive caution from the coach.

sis.personaBrief: The team depended on Varela, Ghiggia, Schiaffino and the keeper's heroics rather than a drilled system, with the captain correcting positions on the pitch. Duties applied to all, yet talent was free to decide games.

jog.personaBrief: Garra and physical contest (metiendo, huevos en la punta de los botines) combined with the technique of Schiaffino and Pérez. Uruguay won through duels and a resilient spirit, at a time when running was expected.

bas.personaBrief: The side was built on seasoned players such as Varela, Máspoli and González, who was restored after a conflict, with 19-year-old Morán an exception. Experience led the way in the decider.

lid.personaBrief: López was calm and conciliatory but the captain Varela effectively overruled him in the dressing room and settled the González dispute himself. Leadership came from the players, and the group's unity mattered.
